newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian MPs diminish their shield of immunity.
newsitem.headline: Belgian MPs diminish their shield of immunity.

text.p: Belgian parliamentarians have adopted changes to the constitution which will make it easier for judges to investigate them but will also keep such probes further away from the public eye.

By 122 to 12, with four abstentions, parliament voted through amendments to the law which will allow the courts to question members or search their offices or houses for evidence without prior approval from parliament as a whole.
The article also applies to government ministers who are technically not members of parliament.

A member's immunity will still have to be lifted by a full session of parliament if a judge seeks an arrest or wants to send the individual before the courts on the grounds that there is adequate evidence to prosecute.

Court requests to parliament for the removal of the protective shield of immunity have been highly-publicised and have in recent cases threatened to bring down parliamentarians even before their peers had weighed up the evidence.

But there have also been concerns that any refusals by parliament to lift immunity could smack of a cover-up, with the governing majority using its weight to protect members of the four coalition parties from prosecution.
The amendments were drafted in the wake of the Di Rupo case in which Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo was accused of having had sex with boys under the age of 16, an offence under Belgian law.
After more than two weeks in which the story rarely left the front pages, parliament decided there was not enough to the allegations to make them stand up in court.
Throughout the affair, Di Rupo said he was innocent and that he had sex only with consulting adults.

The most prominent victim of the 'old' immunity article was NATO secretary general Willy Claes, who was forced to resign from the alliance in 1995 after parliament voted to send him before the courts over allegations he knew of bribes dating back to the late 1980s when he was Belgian economics minister.
